html:
The map's label, in 1880 and 1900, for the northernmost branch of the Ngoni, settled south of Lake Victoria in what is now Tanzania, far from their Nguni homeland in South Africa.

The Ngoni were followers of the chief Zwangendaba, who fled the wars of Shaka in the 1820s, part of the Mfecane. They crossed the Zambezi in 1835 and marched north, absorbing captives as they went. After Zwangendaba died in the 1840s, his people split. One group, known as the Tuta, pushed north into the land of the Nyamwezi and raided as far as the southern shores of Lake Victoria.

Their regiments and stabbing spears spread a new style of war across East Africa. Nyamwezi leaders such as Mirambo copied their methods and hired their fighters. The Germans brought them under German East Africa in the 1890s.
